uncited: The Amira 3D Edge-Preserving Smoothing Filter is a non-linear smoothing method applied to 3D grayscale image stacks to reduce noise while maintaining sharp boundaries between distinct structures.
It addresses the limitation of linear Gaussian smoothing, which blurs edges by averaging across intensity discontinuities.

Unlike the parent [Gaussian Smoothing for Level-Set Extraction](1605-gaussian-smoothing-for-level-set-extraction.md) which uses a fixed kernel, this method dynamically adjusts the convolution kernel based on local image content to prevent edge blurring.
The filter operates on a 3D volume of floating-point intensity values.
It iteratively smooths the volume by varying the convolution kernel size and weights based on the local contrast between neighboring voxels.
- A 3D volume $V$ of size $W \times H \times D$ with floating-point intensity values.
- The volume is stored as a contiguous array or 3D array of floats.
- A temporary buffer is used for intermediate calculations to avoid overwriting input data during iteration.
Calculate the local gradient or intensity difference for each voxel.
Determine the effective kernel size or weights for each voxel based on the local contrast relative to $C$.
If the local intensity difference exceeds $C$, reduce the smoothing influence to preserve the edge.
Apply a weighted 3D convolution to $V_{current}$ using the adaptive weights.
The sigma $\sigma$ controls the base spread of the smoothing.
Update $V_{next}$ with the result of the convolution.
- Boundary conditions: The source does not specify boundary handling.
- Degenerate input: Uniform regions will be smoothed heavily; sharp edges will be preserved.
If the contrast threshold is too low, edges may be blurred.
A linear smoothing method applied to 3D grayscale image stacks.
It performs a three-dimensional convolution with a Gaussian kernel to smooth structures and interpolate borders in less-stretched sections based on neighboring gray values.
It is used for general smoothing and balancing inhomogeneous stretching.
It is chosen when edge preservation is not required and uniform smoothing is sufficient.
It differs from the edge-preserving filter by using a fixed kernel regardless of local content.
- **Time Complexity:** $O(N \cdot K^3)$ per iteration, where $N$ is the number of voxels and $K$ is the kernel size.
The edge-preserving filter requires multiple iterations (up to 25), making it slower than a single-pass Gaussian filter.
- **Memory Complexity:** $O(N)$ for the volume and temporary buffers.
Parameter tuning (contrast, sigma) is required for optimal results.
- **When to use:** When edge preservation is critical, such as in biological imaging where structures have distinct boundaries.
- **When not to use:** When computational speed is paramount and edge blurring is acceptable, or when the volume is already noise-free.
The Amira 3D Edge-Preserving Smoothing Filter is part of the Amira 3D software package (specifically Amira 4.1 as cited).
It was used in the context of volume rendering from serial sections of biological specimens, such as *Cristatella mucedo* and *Phoronis australis*.
